video_title: How To Find The Best Stocks In The Market with Josh Brown
gist: Dan Nathan interviews Ritholtz Wealth CEO Josh Brown amid a sharp AI-complex selloff (Google -13%, Caterpillar -10%, ServiceNow -20% on the day) after hyperscalers like Meta and Oracle stopped ratcheting capex higher. Brown argues the pullback is a healthy derating of high-quality names, lays out his 'start with the best stocks' Russell 1000 leaderboard process and Ritholtz's tax-aware portfolio stack, and floats a thesis that vertically integrated AI players (model + own compute, e.g. Alphabet) will win, while Nathan stresses private-market concentration risk around the Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs.

themes.theme: AI capex plateau and the derating

insights.claim: Josh Brown attributes the current industrial and semiconductor selloff to hyperscalers (Meta, Oracle) signaling they no longer need to ratchet capex budgets materially higher, after roughly seven or eight straight quarters of raises.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A capex plateau, not a demand collapse, is the trigger; watch hyperscaler guidance as the swing factor for AI-supply-chain stocks.
insights.quote: one after another are sort of starting to say, actually, we don't have to take these capex budgets up materially from what we already told you.

insights.claim: Brown says semiconductors are in a bear market and that he welcomes it as healthy, not wanting the S&P at 50x earnings or the Nasdaq at 100x.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Long-only managers see the pullback as an opportunity to buy quality on sale rather than a top.
insights.quote: I think it's why the semiconductors are are in a bare market. I think it's healthy.

insights.claim: Brown cites semiconductor earnings growing about 60-65% year over year this quarter while semi multiples have contracted roughly 20% year to date, and notes Micron trades around five times earnings.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Low multiples on peak-looking earnings show the market is already pricing cyclicality, unlike 1999.
insights.quote: These micron is five times earnings. Everybody is super sober about the possibility that we could be living through peaks right now.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan counters that most semiconductor earnings growth is concentrated in Nvidia and Micron, that names like KLA have already been cut in half, and that earnings were pulled forward so revisions will start moving lower.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: If revisions turn down, the low multiples may be a value trap rather than a bargain.
insights.quote: But they pulled forward all the earnings. I mean that's the point.

insights.claim: Caterpillar is down more than 40% from recent highs after having run up about 300% from its 2025 post-tariff lows, which Brown says was matched by its earnings.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: AI-adjacent industrials can round-trip violently when capex expectations flatten.

insights.claim: Brown argues interest rates are the only reason companies reporting 40-80% earnings growth have flat-to-down stock prices, and that if the S&P tracked earnings growth this year it would be at ludicrous levels.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Earnings growth is outpacing index performance; a rate relief would unlock multiple expansion.
insights.quote: You have companies reporting 40, 60, 80% earnings growth and the stock prices are flat to down. Why? Interest rates. There's no other reason.

insights.claim: Brown says that in a 25% S&P bear market, talk of rate hikes would end, and that the stock market's centrality to the real economy has never been greater, citing GDP growth through a three-year housing recession.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A deep equity drawdown would hit consumer spending and force a policy pivot.
insights.quote: we've created a society that relies on the stock market going up.

insights.claim: Nathan sketches a bear scenario into 2027 where Amazon or Apple disappoint, Anthropic's updated pre-IPO financials look weak or the IPO is pushed out, and Nvidia (late November) and Micron (early December) expose a pull-forward, producing a 25-30% Nasdaq drawdown; Brown calls it entirely possible.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Upcoming catalysts form a concentrated risk calendar for the AI trade.

themes.theme: Mega-cap earnings reads: Google, Meta, Amazon

insights.claim: Brown says Google missed in eight of ten categories, with search growth decelerating to about 12% and YouTube decelerating, reviving the question of whether LLM usage is finally cannibalizing search.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Search deceleration is the first hard evidence for the LLM-cannibalization bear case on Alphabet.
insights.quote: But that search number decelerating is meaningful.

insights.claim: Brown describes Meta as one of the most tortuous stocks to hold over three years, noting that after the Muse launch rally it announced a $100 billion mixed equity raise including non-voting C-class at-the-market shares, a 6.5% convertible preferred due 2029, and $25 billion of common.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The ATM program creates a permanent dilution overhang for Meta shareholders even if raising now is strategically smart.
insights.quote: So for the meta shareholder, it's been a torture chamber.

insights.claim: Nathan notes Meta went from 52-week lows (down 35%) after a capex-driven 10% drop, rallied back to prior highs adding about half a trillion in market cap on the Muse launch, then gave up about two-thirds of that move.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Narrative-driven swings in Meta highlight fragile investor psychology around AI products.

insights.claim: Nathan says none of the roughly 25 college seniors he spoke with were using Meta's Muse and most had never heard of it, despite heavy NFL advertising; Brown counters that Muse targets older heads of household and Meta's 3 billion users give it distribution.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan / Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Early Muse adoption among young users looks weak; distribution, not product edge, is Meta's bull case.

insights.claim: Brown says AI agents like Instinct and Muse became less useful within two to three weeks as airlines, Amazon and other e-commerce platforms blocked bots from completing transactions, while Walmart notably has not blocked them.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Agentic commerce depends on platform access deals; walled gardens are an early bottleneck.
insights.quote: It's becoming less useful because e-commerce platforms and apps are throwing up guardrails to sort of tamp it down.

insights.claim: Brown, who owns Amazon, says the stock's problem is that the Street punishes quarters where expense growth outpaces AWS cloud growth; Nathan thinks AWS is well placed after GCP grew ~100% and Azure ~50%, having not spent hundreds of billions training frontier models.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown / Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: For Amazon, watch AWS growth vs. expense growth as the key earnings tell.
insights.quote: the street hates when expense growth in that quarter outpaces the growth in in cloud.

insights.claim: Nathan says roughly 90% of sell-side analysts rate every Mag 7 stock a strong buy, implying the Street is offsides and few will downgrade Google despite margin risk from spending.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Uniform bullish sell-side ratings leave room for downgrade-driven pressure.

themes.theme: Vertical integration as the AI winner

insights.claim: Brown hypothesizes that AI winners will need to be end-to-end, owning both the model and the compute, which today fits only Google (Gemini plus Google Cloud), Meta (Muse plus its own compute), and partially the Tesla/SpaceX/Grok complex.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: If true, a 10% Alphabet selloff looks like a gift and model-only players face a structural disadvantage.
insights.quote: Something in the back of my head is telling me half is not going to be good enough. I think the winners are going to have to be end to end.

insights.claim: Brown notes Anthropic said in its S-1 it will probably need to build some of its own compute, a new and late development, while OpenAI owns no compute and relies on Microsoft, Oracle leases and commitments.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Owning compute becomes a new capex burden and strategic imperative for model labs.
insights.quote: Anthropic said in the S1 that they probably are going to have to build some compute of their own.

insights.claim: Brown warns Amazon could be in trouble if vertical integration wins, since its Bedrock strategy is 'bring your own model' rather than owning a premier model.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Platform-neutral cloud strategies may lose share if model+compute bundling becomes decisive.

insights.claim: Brown suggests a cash-rich Anthropic (about $200 billion in cash post-IPO and a ~$1.5 trillion stock currency) could acquire distressed neoclouds like CoreWeave (in a 60% drawdown) or Nebius rather than rent compute indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Beaten-down neocloud equity could see takeout optionality from cash-flush model labs.
insights.quote: we could build compute from scratch or we can rescue one of these debt laden companies that doesn't have their together

insights.claim: Brown dismisses worries about data-center SPVs, CDS and rising financing costs, arguing token demand is the key ingredient and is not reversing, and that if a neocloud fails its facility will be absorbed by someone else.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Credit stress hits equity of weak players, not the physical AI build-out itself.
insights.quote: The key ingredient is demand for tokens and AI. It is not going to reverse.

insights.claim: Brown argues that if AI project funding froze (private credit, Blackstone, Asian chip billionaires stop funding), the three existing hyperscalers and Meta would benefit, and chips, memory and electricity would get cheaper, making AI cheaper for everyone.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A funding freeze is a moat-widening event for incumbents and a deflationary tailwind for AI users.
insights.quote: AI will become freer and cheaper to use.

insights.claim: Brown says the right question is not bond demand for data centers but who monetizes AI best across power companies, construction/capital equipment (Caterpillar, Quanta), chipmakers, Korean memory, software and agentic apps, and that nobody knows yet.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Value-chain capture is the open question; diversify across layers rather than betting on one.

insights.claim: Nathan argues private markets have never dictated public-market sentiment as much, with Anthropic and OpenAI having made one to two trillion dollars of compute commitments, creating a single point of failure for the AI supply chain.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The public AI complex depends on two private companies' ability to meet obligations.
insights.quote: there is a single point of failure as it relates to those two companies and their ability to meet those obligations

insights.claim: Brown says Anthropic is expected to IPO at $1.5-2 trillion raising about $100 billion (likely upsized to ~$120 billion), having already raised $140 billion privately, making it and another listing the two largest IPOs ever within six months.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Mega-IPOs will become immediate top-15 index weights, absorbing large amounts of capital.

insights.claim: Brown says Anthropic's headline ~$80 billion loss in the first half is an accounting treatment, and that operating loss fell from $2.1 billion on $1.2 billion revenue in 1H last year to $690 million on $16 billion revenue in 1H this year (about 1,300% revenue growth).
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Underlying operating trajectory is far better than headlines suggest, though lease commitments remain the real scrutiny point.
insights.quote: So, it's 1300% revenue growth and operating loss negative 58%.

insights.claim: Brown says Elon Musk's Tesla is possibly the last company to go from a ~$10 billion market cap to a trillion dollars in public hands, because today companies like Anthropic, OpenAI and Cerebras (IPO'd at ~$100 billion) come public at enormous valuations.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Retail investors and small-cap indices no longer capture early-stage growth; the Russell 2000 is no longer a proxy for it.
insights.quote: He's the last guy to build a trillion dollar company that public shareholders, moms and pops, >> had the ability to benefit from.

insights.claim: Nathan doubts there is much incremental demand for the Anthropic IPO, saying private-market insiders and employees have been heavy secondary sellers, the founders are not likable, and the big mutual fund complexes already own it; Brown disagrees and expects retail enthusiasm.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: IPO demand depth is a key uncertainty for the largest-ever listings.
insights.quote: if you are in the private world you want to sell you're not a buyer right now

insights.claim: Brown notes lockups are now staggered (Cerebras as a test run for SpaceX: first tranche after five weeks, then monthly), eliminating the classic short-into-unlock trade, and index inclusion now happens much faster.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The old lockup-expiry short playbook is less reliable for mega-IPOs.

insights.claim: Brown says Sam Altman owning no OpenAI stock bothers him, speculating he benefits more by steering OpenAI deals toward his other startups.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Governance and alignment concerns could weigh on OpenAI's eventual IPO reception.
insights.quote: his explanation is always so bullshitty

themes.theme: Ritholtz portfolio process and stock selection

insights.claim: Brown's stock universe is the Russell 1000, from which a multi-factor screen (quality, technical setup, positive earnings, sales growth) currently yields about 140 'best stocks', with Apple the only Mag 7 name on the list.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Momentum-plus-quality leaderboards are a disciplined starting point for idea generation.
insights.quote: If you want to buy a stock because it's going to go up, start with a stock that's already going up.

insights.claim: Brown says the most common investor mistake is having no starting point, building 'salad' portfolios from TV tips, relatives and articles, instead of starting from the market's current leaders.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Process over tips: start from winners and understand why they lead.
insights.quote: Why would you start with a 52e low list?

insights.claim: Brown says the 130/30 fund category raised about $150 billion year over year because losses were so scarce in 2024-2025 that wealthy clients needed vehicles to manufacture tax losses, with AQR a big player.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Loss-scarcity drove a boom in leveraged long/short tax strategies, a sign of an extended bull run.
insights.quote: Losses were so scarce that people were inventing and funding vehicles to deliberately create loss.

insights.claim: Brown calls custom indexing the biggest investing revolution since the ETF; Ritholtz has put over $1 billion into it over five years to tax-loss harvest while tracking the index.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Direct indexing is becoming core for high-net-worth after-tax returns.
insights.quote: This is probably the biggest revolution in investing since the ETF.

insights.claim: Brown says Ritholtz launched a new strategy called Porterhouse this summer that already has $100 million, owning market leadership but able to move positions to cash rather than own second- and third-best stocks.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Advisors are productizing momentum/leadership strategies with cash as a risk valve.

insights.claim: Brown says the S&P 500 is effectively the greatest momentum strategy ever, since index construction makes winners like Apple dominate while losers shrink, and that for young accumulators there is no better approach.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Concentration (top 10 near 40% of S&P, 50% of Nasdaq 100) is a feature of momentum, not a bug, for long horizons.
insights.quote: the S&P 500 is it's effectively the greatest momentum strategy in the history of uh the markets.

insights.claim: Brown cites the S&P averaging about 12.5% annual returns including dividends over the 17 years since the financial crisis, calling it possibly the greatest bull market of his lifetime.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Return expectations anchored to this period may be too high going forward.

insights.claim: Brown states as an iron rule that anything done over the long term to limit volatility will cap upside returns.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Volatility reduction is a cost to be chosen deliberately, not a free benefit.
insights.quote: Anything that you do over the long term to limit volatility will 100% cap the upside of your potential returns.

insights.claim: Brown bets the median 60/40 client of financial advisors custodied at Schwab has outperformed the global macro hedge fund universe after fees, and says investing on political or election views has been a 'dead bang loser' since 2016.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Macro and geopolitical forecasting adds little value versus disciplined allocation.
